title: Sweetgreen Cuts Full-Year Outlook as Cyclospora Outbreak Tanks Salad Demand
excerpt: The salad chain slashed its same-store sales forecast and warned of prolonged consumer hesitancy toward fresh produce, even though none of its ingredients have been linked to the nationwide illness.
body:
• Sweetgreen now expects same-store sales to fall 7–8% in fiscal 2026, nearly double its previous forecast of a 2–4% decline, citing the multistate cyclosporiasis outbreak.
  • Second-quarter revenue rose 3.8% to $192.7 million but missed Wall Street estimates; the chain lost 22 cents per share, worse than the 15-cent loss analysts expected.
  • The company also issued a voluntary jalapeno recall tied to a separate salmonella investigation, compounding food-safety pressure on the brand.
  • Stock plunged roughly 15% in after-hours trading Thursday, extending a nearly 30% decline over the past month.

Sweetgreen slashed its full-year outlook on Thursday after the largest cyclosporiasis outbreak in U.S. history rattled consumers away from salads and other fresh prepared foods — even at chains with no confirmed connection to the illness.

The fast-casual salad chain said it now expects same-store sales to drop 7% to 8% for fiscal 2026, roughly double the 2% to 4% decline it had guided in May. Restaurant-level margins were cut to a projected 10.5% to 11%, down sharply from the earlier range of 14.2% to 14.7%, according to the company's earnings release.

A Clean Bill — But a Guilty Verdict From the Market

CEO Jonathan Neman emphasized during the earnings call that Sweetgreen does not use iceberg lettuce — the product identified in the federal investigation — and that the company has received "no indication from our suppliers or public-health authorities that Sweetgreen is connected to that outbreak."

The reassurance did little to stop the bleeding. Shares tumbled roughly 15% in after-hours trading, extending a nearly 30% slide over the past month as investors treated the outbreak as a sector-wide demand risk, Barron's reported.

"Our results are not where they need to be, but the progress we saw in the second quarter reinforces our confidence that the plan is working."

— Jonathan Neman, CEO, Sweetgreen

Second Quarter: Revenue Grows, But From New Stores

For the quarter ended in June, revenue rose 3.8% from a year earlier to $192.7 million, slightly below the $194.5 million expected by analysts polled by FactSet. Same-store sales fell 6.2%, with foot traffic down 2% and average ticket size shrinking 4.2% due to heavier promotions and customers trading down to lower-priced items such as wraps.

Sweetgreen lost 22 cents per share during the quarter — two cents more than the year-ago period and worse than Wall Street's estimate of a 15-cent loss, the Wall Street Journal reported. Restaurant-level margin contracted by nearly six percentage points to 13.1%, hurt by weaker comparable sales and higher ingredient costs tied to larger chicken and tofu portions.

Adjusted EBITDA expectations also swung dramatically: the company now projects a loss of $23 million to $27 million for the full year, compared with a previous forecast of $1 million to $6 million in profit.

A Second Food-Safety Blow

Compounding the cyclospora headwind, Sweetgreen disclosed a voluntary recall of jalapenos from one supplier in "affected areas" the day before earnings. The recall is tied to a separate salmonella outbreak under investigation across multiple states that has also prompted Chipotle and Qdoba to pull jalapenos from their menus, MarketWatch reported.

Neman said jalapenos appeared in only two of the chain's dressings and nowhere else on its menu, and that it was too early to assess the financial impact of the recall.

Silver Linings Before the Storm

Before the cyclospora scare upended consumer confidence in mid-July, Sweetgreen's turnaround had been gaining traction. Same-store sales trends improved from a 12.8% decline in the prior quarter, and foot-traffic tracker Placer.ai estimated that visits rose 1% in May and 3.9% in June, driven partly by a nationwide wrap launch.

Michigan health authorities said Thursday that residents could "resume routine guidance" for eating salads as new cyclosporiasis cases begin to fall, offering a potential turning point. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported more than 1,644 confirmed cases across at least 34 states since May, with thousands more under review.

What's Next

Sweetgreen plans to open 13 new restaurants this year, with roughly half featuring its Infinite Kitchen robotic system. But investors now face a central question: whether the food-safety shock fades quickly enough for the chain's operational improvements to matter, or whether consumer anxiety about fresh produce lingers through the back half of the year.

The stock has erased all of its 2026 gains and closed at $5.87 ahead of the earnings release.
